unitDescription.value:
In this unit, students develop practical woodworking and design skills through the production of a timber desk organiser. Students learn to safely select and use hand tools, power equipment and workshop processes to accurately measure, mark, cut, join, assemble and finish timber components. The project introduces box joints, timber properties, sanding and varnishing techniques, as well as the Lean 5S principles for creating an organised and efficient workspace.

Alongside the practical project, students follow the SBC Design Model to develop an improved desk-organiser concept suited to their own study needs. They investigate existing products, generate ideas, produce dimensioned isometric drawings and evaluate their design against the requirements of the design brief.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: Students at St Brendan’s College operate within a diverse learning environment where practical, hands-on application is essential to engagement and skill acquisition. The Year 7–8 Design Technologies curriculum is structured to accommodate varying levels of prior experience with digital systems and manual production techniques. Learning experiences leverage the College’s commitment to vocational pathways and technical literacy, ensuring that students develop fundamental design-thinking skills alongside an appreciation for safety, sustainability, and material performance. Tasks are designed to build student confidence through scaffolded inquiry and iterative prototyping, providing frequent opportunities for students to connect design solutions to authentic, real-world community contexts. Literacy and numeracy support is integrated across all units, ensuring students can effectively communicate design proposals and analyse project data. Teachers differentiate instruction to support the specific needs of the cohort, fostering resilience and independent problem-solving through reflective practice and iterative design cycles that align with the achievement standards of the Australian Curriculum.

description.value:
Students complete two connected assessment components:

Practical project: Construct a functional timber desk organiser based on the supplied workshop design. Students are assessed on their safe workshop practices, accurate measurement and marking, production of box joints, assembly techniques, surface preparation, application of finishes and overall quality of the completed product.
Design and theory folio: Complete a digital folio documenting workshop safety, woodworking knowledge, Lean 5S principles and the development of an improved desk-organiser design. Students define the design problem, investigate existing organisers, identify useful design features, brainstorm ideas, produce a draft isometric sketch, self-evaluate their proposal and submit a final annotated and dimensioned design drawing. The design must be unique, provide storage for frequently used study items and must not include storage for a mobile phone.

conditions.value:
• Practical project: 6 weeks of workshop-based construction; assessed through direct teacher observation of safe, independent use of hand and power tools.
• Design and theory folio: Maximum 6 A4 pages or equivalent digital portfolio, including annotated isometric sketches, technical drawings, and reflective commentary.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 8 students explain how people design, innovate and produce products, services and environments for preferred futures. For each of the 4 prescribed technologies contexts they explain how the features of technologies impact on design decisions, and create designed solutions based on analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create and adapt design ideas, processes and solutions, and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas and solutions to audiences using technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools. They independently and collaboratively document and manage production processes to safely produce designed solutions.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically within the Design Technologies department to ensure consistent, evidence-based judgements aligned with the Australian Curriculum achievement standards. This process involves:

*   **Moderation Conferencing:** Scheduled collaborative sessions at Weeks 4 and 8 to review samples of student folios and practical products, ensuring a shared understanding of the marking guide criteria.
*   **Cross-marking:** Departmental review of the Design and Theory Folio to ensure objective application of quality standards regarding technical drawing accuracy and design evaluation.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students are inducted into the workshop, establishing the foundational safety protocols and behavioral expectations required for a productive learning environment. The week focuses on the St Brendan’s College 'Gold Standard' for workshop safety and an introduction to the Lean 5S principles (Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain) as a mechanism for workplace efficiency. Students examine the desk organiser project exemplar to deconstruct its assembly flow and material requirements, setting the stage for their individual design journeys.

theory.value: Explicit teaching of WHS regulations, including hazard identification, risk assessment, and the mandatory use of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). Students are introduced to the Lean 5S system and how these organisational principles mitigate waste and improve production precision in a woodworking context. The exemplar is analysed to explain the relationship between design features and manufacturing sequences, ensuring students understand the project's technical scope and structural integrity.

prac.value: Students complete the required OnGuard safety induction modules to earn their workshop access licence. Practical sessions involve a guided tour of the machinery zone, learning the 'Safe Operating Procedure' (SOP) for basic hand tools. Students engage in a 5S audit of their own workstation, labelling tools and clearing hazards to mirror professional cabinet-making practices.

assessment.value: Formative: Completion of OnGuard safety modules and teacher observation of initial workshop conduct. Students provide an annotated 'Safety First' checklist entry in their digital folios.

outlineTheme.value: Students are introduced to the workshop environment, safety culture and the fundamental principles of the Lean 5S system. They examine the desk organiser exemplar to understand its structure, material requirements and assembly flow while completing mandatory OnGuard safety modules.

question: What is the critical distinction between a hazard and a risk in our woodwork shop?
expected: A hazard is an object or situation with potential to cause harm, whereas risk is the likelihood and severity of that harm occurring.

expected: It outlines the verified, sequential safety controls necessary to prevent operator injury and machine damage.

activities.title: Lean 5S Methodology in Manufacturing
activities.teacherDoes: Present the Lean 5S framework (Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain) using cabinet-making workshop photos. Model the distinction between 'Sort' (Seiri — discarding or returning unneeded materials) and 'Set in Order' (Seiton — arranging necessary tools in shadow boards for instant access). Emphasise how 5S directly improves manufacturing precision and cuts wasted production time.

activities.questioning:
How does implementing 'Set in Order' (Seiton) directly reduce manufacturing mistakes during timber marking out? Expected: Tools such as try squares and marking gauges have dedicated, clean locations so they are not dropped, misaligned, or lost under timber shavings.
Why is 'Sustain' considered the most difficult 5S principle to achieve in a shared school workshop? Expected: It requires disciplined, consistent daily habits from every student group rather than relying on an occasional deep clean.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Part A (5S Recommendations):
1. Sort: Remove all scrap timber off-cuts and unrelated project parts from the bench top and place them in the off-cut bin.
2. Set in Order: Position measuring tools (rule, try square) on the upper bench well with cutting tools facing downward.
3. Shine & Standardise: Sweep bench surface clear of timber dust before marking out, ensuring glue bottles are capped and stored in upright holders.

Part B (Exemplar Components):
1. Four-sided radiata pine outer perimeter frame joined by interlocking box/finger joints.
2. 3mm or 6mm manufactured board (plywood/MDF) base panel fitted into a recessed rebate.

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why does a loose knot present a major risk during joinery construction?
expected: Loose knots have broken wood fibres and lack bonding to the surrounding timber; when cut, routed, or chiselled, they fall out completely and ruin the joint.
prompt: What causes an end split in timber stock, and how do we manage it in the workshop?
expected: Rapid moisture loss through exposed end-grain fibres causes radial splitting; the split section must be docked (cut off) during sizing before measuring components.
activities.scaffolding:

- Straight grain: Parallel fibres running the length of the board, ideal for structural stability and clean cutting.
- End split (check): Separation along the growth rings caused by rapid drying at the ends; requires docking past the crack.
- Loose knot: Dead branch remnant surrounded by a dark bark ring; not bonded to surrounding wood and prone to falling out.
- Cupping: Curvature across the face (width) of the board caused by uneven moisture loss.

activities.title: Modelled Sawing: Stance, Grip, and Kerf Management
activities.teacherDoes: Stand at the demonstration bench with a back-saw and bench hook. Explicitly model setup: timber firmly pressed against the bench hook stop, non-sawing hand safely behind the cut line. Model the grip: dominant hand holding the saw handle with index finger pointed along the brass spine for directional tracking. Demonstrate starting the cut on the waste side of the knife line using gentle backward draw-strokes at a 20-degree angle. Highlight: 'Notice the saw kerf is the thickness of the blade teeth; cutting centered on the line loses 1.5mm of component length.'

q: Why must the index finger extend along the back spine of the saw handle?
Expected: It aligns the forearm muscles with the blade to prevent twisting and keep the cut vertical.
q: Why must the cut be initiated strictly on the waste side of the marking line?
Expected: The saw kerf removes material; cutting on the waste side leaves the component at the exact required dimension.
activities.scaffolding: Reference callout points: 1. Index finger along brass back (tracks cutting line); 2. Thumb guide on waste side (stabilises starting stroke); 3. Stance at 45 degrees to bench (allows straight arm swing); 4. Bench hook stop shoulder (resists forward sawing force).

activities.title: Modelled Audit: Using the Combination Square
activities.teacherDoes: Model the diagnostic audit procedure under the document camera. Hold the machined face of the combination square stock firmly against the timber datum edge ('face edge'). Gently slide the blade down until it spans the end grain. Point out: 'Look toward the light. If you see a sliver of light between the steel blade and the end grain, the edge is out of square. An angle error of just 1 degree will produce a visible compound gap when the sides are joined.' Demonstrate the four critical inspection locations on the component.

q: Why must the square's stock be pressed against an established face edge rather than an unverified cut edge?
Expected: The face edge is flat and true; using an unverified edge introduces compounding measurement errors.
activities.scaffolding: Diagnostic terms: Datum edge = true reference face; Stock = cast-iron body resting on reference surface; Blade = precision steel rule perpendicular at 90 degrees; Light gap = visible gap indicating deviation from true perpendicularity.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the structural science of box joints using timber demonstration blocks. Explain how timber fibres act like bundles of straws: end-grain absorbs adhesive without forming a strong bond, whereas side-grain (long-grain) to side-grain contact creates a massive surface area for PVA glue to form a molecular bond. activities.questioning:
q: Why does a butt joint fail easily when pulled apart, even with wood glue?
Expected: The joint relies on end-grain adhesion, which starves the joint because porous fibres draw glue away from the contact plane.
q: Why does the marking gauge baseline need to equal the exact timber thickness of the joining board?
Expected: So that the protruding fingers sit perfectly flush with the adjacent timber face once assembled, requiring minimal sanding.

activities.title: Chisel Safety SOP & Saw kerf Position
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate at the front vice how to saw strictly on the waste side of the pencil line, leaving the line visible (maintaining the 20mm finger width). Demonstrate chisel safety: secure timber firmly in the vice; keep both hands behind the cutting edge at all times; never chisel towards your body. Model chopping the waste: place the bevel facing into the waste, chisel halfway down from side A, flip the timber in the vice, and chisel from side B to eliminate grain tear-out and shoulder blow-out.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each chisel and sawing action to its safety and technical reason in the table by writing the correct definition from the bank.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must the saw blade sit entirely on the waste side of the pencil line?
expected: Because the saw kerf removes 1mm to 1.5mm of wood; cutting on the line would make the pin undersized and the joint loose.
question: Why do we chisel halfway through from both sides rather than driving the chisel all the way through from one side?
expected: Driving straight through will tear out and splinter the timber fibres on the exit face, ruining the joint shoulder.
activities.scaffolding:
Safety & Technical Rules:
1. Hands behind the blade: Prevents severe lacerations if the tool slips.
2. Timber in vice: Prevents workpiece movement during striking.
3. Halfway channelling: Prevents grain blowout and splitting on the exit face.
4. Kerf on waste side: Maintains the full finished dimension of the pin.

Expected: It forces timber fibres into close contact and expels air pockets to create a thin, uniform adhesive line.

activities.title: Teacher Clamping and Cleanup Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes:
Demonstrate the complete sash clamp setup on a timber carcass at the front bench. Show how steel clamp teeth bruise timber without pine scrap cauls. Demonstrate measuring opposing diagonal corners with a steel tape rule to prove squareness (e.g., both 317 mm). Demonstrate removing wet squeeze-out using a cabinet scraper held at 45 degrees followed by a damp cotton rag.

Modelled Narrative:
'Watch closely as I dry-fit this carcass. Notice how I place soft pine scrap cauls between the hard steel clamp jaw and our finished workpiece surface; without these, the high clamping pressure will crush our timber fibres. Now, as I apply tension to the sash clamps, I check squareness immediately by measuring diagonal corner to corner. Both diagonals read exactly 317 mm, confirming our frame is square. Finally, I take my cabinet scraper at a 45-degree angle to slice away the tacky PVA squeeze-out before following up with a damp cotton rag to ensure no glue residue remains to ruin our final finish.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, noting caul placement, diagonal measurement technique, and scraper angle. Complete the 5-point verification checklist in your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the clamping demonstration at the front bench. Tick off each procedural check on your checklist as it is demonstrated.
activities.questioning:
What physical damage occurs if steel sash clamps are tightened directly against our timber carcass?
Expected: The hard steel faces will crush the timber fibres, leaving deep, irreparable indentations.

Why does measuring diagonal corners prove whether our rectangular carcass is square?
Expected: In a true rectangle, opposite diagonals are identical; unequal diagonals indicate a skewed parallelogram.
activities.scaffolding:
Caul: A scrap timber block placed between the clamp jaw and workpiece to spread pressure and prevent bruising.
Squeeze-out: The bead of excess PVA glue forced out of a joint when pressure is applied.
Open Time: The maximum time allowed between applying PVA glue and final clamp tightening (typically 5–10 minutes).

activities.title: Timber Cellular Anatomy & Defect Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Place a magnified softwood end-grain block under the document camera. Script: 'Observe these hollow tubular cells called tracheids. End-grain acts like a bundle of drinking straws, drawing liquids rapidly via capillary action. When a saw blade cuts against these tubes, it causes tear-out. Timber filler is formulated to bridge these gaps, but if it is applied poorly, it will pull away during curing.' Model defining the terms accurately on the whiteboard.

activities.questioning:
question: Why does timber end-grain absorb stain and moisture significantly faster than tangential face-grain?
Expected: End-grain exposes open longitudinal cellular vessels (tracheids) that draw liquids through capillary action, whereas face-grain presents sealed cellular walls.
question: What causes timber tear-out during machining or sawing operations?
Expected: Cutting forces lifting and breaking longitudinal wood fibres along natural cleavage lines rather than shearing them cleanly.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
1. End-Grain: The transverse cross-section of timber exposing the open ends of longitudinal growth cells and vascular tracheids.
2. Tear-out: Severe surface damage occurring when cutting tools lift, rip, or fracture timber fibres along the grain.
3. Timber Filler: A specialised compound of synthetic resin binders and fine wood flour formulated to fill voids, defects, and joint margins.

activities.title: Abrasive Grit Sequencing Protocol
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate abrasive paper selection at the teacher workbench. Script: 'Abrasive grit numbers represent the number of sieve mesh openings per linear inch. 80 grit is coarse and rapidly levels hardened putty mounds. 120 grit removes the deep gouges left by 80 grit. 180 grit refines the face, and 240 grit polishes the fibres before varnishing. If you skip a grit—jumping straight from 80 to 240—the fine paper merely glazes over deep trenches. Always wrap paper tightly around a cork block. Direct fingertip pressure dishes soft summerwood and rounds square joint edges.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration, examine the abrasive grit backing stamps, and order the four sanding stages into the workbook ranking task.

activities.questioning:
What occurs structurally to the wood surface if an 80-grit pass is followed immediately by 240-grit paper? Expected: The fine 240 grit cannot reach the valley floors of the coarse 80-grit scratches, leaving visible permanent scars beneath the varnish.
Why must sanding be performed strictly parallel to the timber grain direction? Expected: Cross-grain motion severs wood fibres transversely, leaving scratches that absorb stain unevenly and become highly visible under clear finish coats.
activities.scaffolding:
The Four Sanding Stages:
1. 80 Grit (Coarse): Level hardened putty mounds flush with timber.
2. 120 Grit (Medium): Erase 80-grit scratch marks and machine marks.
3. 180 Grit (Fine): Remove micro-scratches and smooth timber face.
4. 240 Grit (Extra Fine): Final surface polish and fibre burnish before clear coating.

activities.title: Wood Finishing & Chemical Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce clear finishing terminology using the whiteboard and exemplar varnished timber panels. Explain resin matrices, volatile organic compound (VOC) evaporation, and grain raising. activities.studentsDo: Match the three technical chemical finishing terms to their correct definitions in the workbook table using the definition bank.

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why does clear varnish form an impermeable moisture barrier while raw timber absorbs water?
expected: Varnish cures into a continuous cross-linked polymer film that seals porous timber vessels against ambient water vapour.
prompt: What chemical reaction makes crumpled oil- or solvent-soaked rags a critical workshop fire hazard?
expected: The curing process involves exothermic oxidation; if rags are balled up, heat cannot dissipate, causing spontaneous combustion.
activities.scaffolding:
Term Definitions:
1. Clear Varnish: A solution of resin and solvent that cures to produce a hard, transparent protective barrier.
2. Grain Raising: The swelling and stiffening of severed timber surface fibres when wetted by liquid finishes.
3. Spontaneous Combustion: Ignition occurring without an external flame due to rapid internal heat buildup from chemical oxidation.

activities.title: Modelled First-Coat Brush Technique
activities.teacherDoes:
At the central demonstration bench, model the 'load, lay-on, lay-off' stroke sequence. Demonstrate loading the brush to exactly one-third bristle depth against the pot rim. Show how to lay on the finish across grain, then immediately lay off with long, feather-light strokes parallel to the grain. Demonstrate maintaining a continuous wet edge.

Modelled Script:
'Notice how I only dip the bristles one-third of the way in. If you submerge them to the ferrule, varnish gets trapped inside, drips constantly, and ruins the brush as it dries. Watch the lay-on: cross-grain application distributes the volume quickly. Now, the lay-off: feather-light tips trailing along the grain to remove all ridges. Keep your wet edge moving—never go back over a surface once it starts to tack off.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled brush technique, annotating the technical diagram in their workbooks with the correct terminology for each phase of the stroke cycle.
activities.visibleInstructions: Watch the modelled brush sequence. Annotate your workbook diagram by writing the correct technique phase next to each numbered callout.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do we dip bristles only one-third deep rather than fully submerging them to the ferrule?
expected: Submerging allows varnish to enter the metal ferrule where it cannot be wiped off, causing heavy dripping, wasted finish, and stiff bristles upon drying.
q: What happens if you drag your brush back over an area that has started to tack off?
expected: The tacky film tears and pulls, leaving permanent brush ridges that will not self-level.
activities.scaffolding:
Stroke Sequence Callouts:
1. Bristle Loading: Dip only the tip 1/3 into varnish; gently touch against rim to remove excess.
2. Laying-On: Distribute finish across the surface in short strokes.
3. Laying-Off: Light, continuous strokes along the grain direction to level out the coat.
4. Wet Edge: Maintaining a continuous wet boundary to prevent overlap lines.

activities.title: Topcoat Readiness & Stroke Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher models checking the sanded surface under strong side-lighting to ensure no dust particles are present. The teacher then demonstrates how to load a soft-bristle brush minimally and apply the varnish in long, continuous strokes, maintaining a 'wet-edge' to avoid overlaps. Modelled example: 'Notice how the brush is held at a 45-degree angle, and the stroke follows the longitudinal grain of the Radiata pine without stopping mid-surface.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the live demonstration of brush loading, stroke feathering, and edge control. Complete the pre-application verification checklist in the workbook.

activities.questioning: Why do we apply the final coat with a much lighter touch and less varnish than the sealing coat? Expected: It introduces air bubbles and creates visible brush marks that spoil the smooth finish.
activities.scaffolding: Pre-coat criteria displayed on board: 1. Dust-free surface (tack cloth inspected); 2. 240-grit de-nibbing complete; 3. Minimal brush loading (dip only 1/3 of bristles); 4. Longitudinal grain-aligned strokes.

q: Why is it critical to assess the surface quality before applying the topcoat?

activities.title: Constructing an Objective Evaluation Passage
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher models how to draft a professional evaluation paragraph by contrasting subjective language ('It looks good') with objective technical statements ('The joint is flush to within 0.5mm with a uniform varnish gloss'). The teacher guides the class through the cloze passage, highlighting how each word from the bank anchors the evaluation in measurable evidence. For example, 'When writing about your timber desk organiser, avoid saying the finish is nice; instead, specify that the surface achieves an even gloss free from sanding marks.'

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do professional designers avoid subjective descriptors like 'good' or 'nice' in their final evaluation reports?

expected: Utility describes how effectively the compartments hold stationery items and satisfy functional needs, whereas aesthetics refers to surface finish, timber grain, and visual balance.

Expected: Varnish-soaked rags can undergo exothermic oxidation and spontaneously combust, creating a severe workshop fire hazard in contact with sawdust.

Expected: Clearing sawdust immediately exposes oil leaks, damaged power leads, dull cutting edges, or cracked safety guards on machinery.

activities.questioning:
q: Why does Radiata pine timber have a significantly lower embodied carbon footprint than an equivalent steel or acrylic desk organiser?
Expected: Pine trees absorb and sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide while growing, and timber processing requires far less energy than smelting steel or synthesizing polymers.
q: How does applying a high-quality varnish topcoat represent material stewardship?
Expected: The varnish seals the timber against moisture, grime, and wear, drastically extending the product's usable lifespan and delaying disposal.
activities.scaffolding: Lifecycle stages summary: 1. Plantation & carbon capture; 2. Sustainable harvest & milling; 3. Manufacturing & low-waste assembly; 4. Use & re-coating; 5. Re-use, chipping, or composting. Stewardship = ethical management of resources throughout their life.
activities.eLearning: Projector displays a circular economy flowchart contrasting sustainable timber stewardship with single-use plastic disposal pathways.
activities.transition: Put down your pens and prepare for our final unit wrap-up.
